abstracts.abstract: This paper presents a fundamental reconceptualization of light transport theory through the lens of optimal transport, introducing a novel computational framework that unifies rendering, shading, and image synthesis under a single mathematical formalism. Traditional rendering algorithms rely on either path integral formulations or discrete diffusion approximations, creating a dichotomy that limits algorithmic expressiveness. Our approach establishes that the Radiative Transfer Equation can be reformulated as a gradient flow problem on the space of light distributions, enabling the application of Riemannian optimization techniques previously unexplored in computer graphics. We derive novel sampling strategies emerging from geodesic computations in light path space, demonstrating that this perspective naturally produces unbiased estimators with dramatically reduced variance in challenging illumination scenarios. The theoretical framework extends to participating media and subsurface scattering, where we prove equivalence between our formulation and established physically based simulation methods. Experimental validation on complex scenes with multi-bounce indirect illumination shows our approach achieves order-of-magnitude improvements in convergence rates compared to state-of-the-art path guiding techniques. This work establishes optimal transport as a foundational theory for the next generation of rendering algorithms, opening research directions in adaptive sampling, material representation, and differentiable rendering that were previously inaccessible through conventional theoretical lenses.

We present a rigorous theoretical analysis of texture synthesis algorithms that reveals fundamental limitations in current statistical matching approaches, and derive an improved theoretical framework with provable convergence guarantees. Previous methods based on Markov Random Field or patch-based optimization suffer from boundary artifacts and limited capture of high-frequency geometric details essential for photorealistic rendering. Our analysis establishes connections between texture synthesis and optimal transport theory, demonstrating that existing L2-based similarity metrics systematically fail to preserve perceptual texture properties. We introduce a Wasserstein-based formulation that more accurately captures human perception of texture similarity, along with a hierarchical optimization strategy with O(n log n) complexity. The theoretical analysis also provides bounds on synthesis quality as a function of patch size and overlap constraints, enabling principled algorithm parameter selection. Experimental evaluation on both procedural and photographed textures demonstrates significant improvements in visual quality metrics while maintaining interactive performance. Furthermore, we show applications to geometry processing, where the improved texture analysis enables superior detail preservation in mesh parameterization and normal map synthesis. This work provides both theoretical understanding and practical tools for high-quality texture synthesis in computer graphics applications.

We introduce a complete real-time rendering system that fundamentally reimagines the rendering pipeline for virtual and augmented reality applications by integrating neural rendering directly into the graphics hardware pipeline. Existing VR/AR systems rely on traditional rasterization followed by post-processing, creating a latency bottleneck that fundamentally limits immersion. Our system, NeuralVR, executes differentiable rendering kernels as first-class citizens within a novel GPU architecture designed specifically for neural image synthesis. The system maintains a continuous scene representation that enables physically based simulation of complex materials and lighting at 120Hz with sub-frame latency. We design novel hardware acceleration structures that support dynamic scene modifications without pipeline stalls, enabling real-time interactive graphics with neural quality. The complete system includes tools for content creation, with a custom shading language that abstracts neural rendering complexity while exposing fine-grained control over material and lighting parameters. Benchmarks on challenging VR scenarios including global illumination, soft shadows, and complex geometry demonstrate that NeuralVR achieves quality comparable to offline rendering while maintaining real-time performance requirements. This work establishes a new paradigm for graphics hardware and software co-design that will shape future immersive computing platforms.

We present an improved system for procedural geometry modeling and physically based simulation that significantly advances the state of the art in creating complex animated content. Existing procedural modeling tools suffer from tedious parameter tuning and limited support for physically plausible deformation, requiring artists to manually ensure simulation stability. Our system, PhysProc, integrates procedural generation with real-time physically based simulation through a novel bidirectional editing paradigm where parameter changes immediately reflect in both the geometric model and its physical simulation. The system employs a carefully optimized sparse linear solver that achieves 10x speedup over previous CPU-based approaches while maintaining numerical stability for large-scale deformations. We introduce constraint-aware parameterization techniques that enable intuitive control over geometric complexity without compromising simulation accuracy. The animation subsystem supports multi-resolution simulation with automatic LOD management, ensuring consistent visual quality across varying scene complexity. Evaluation through production deployment with professional animators demonstrates that PhysProc reduces iteration time by 60% while improving physical accuracy, particularly for cloth simulation and soft body dynamics. The system scales from single-object scenes to complex environments with thousands of interacting bodies, maintaining real-time feedback for interactive editing. This work provides a practical tool that bridges the gap between artistic control and physical correctness in computational design workflows.
